items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: The head of Columbia Records was Goddard Lieberson, worked in the English music halls. He played piano and would do a dance for you. He was an artist.

ctx.x: How has recording changed from then ‘til now for you?

Well, a lot. A lot. I think in the first place, not just recording but the whole music industry. In those days the music industry was wisely left to the artists, you know. The heads of the all the record companies were musicians and artists. They had their business departments with their lawyers and their bookkeepers and their bean counters and all, they were there. But the decisions, you know, that affected the work, were made by artists, so that you had great productivity from all the record companies. The guy,…
That’s kind of a shame. But you still manage to put out some good product. And it’s wonderful, like you have your family singing with you. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: when I was recording for Columbia, the head of Columbia was Goddard Lieberson... had the sympathy and the dedication to try to promote the arts

ctx.x: Jon, what are your thoughts about jazz as an American national treasure and the whole arts environment and its impact upon American society?

I think that we – jazz artists, jazz itself – we’re under attack. We’re like a city that’s being bombed, like Guernica in the Spanish Civil War, where the Germans used their new Stuka bomber just to test it out. Those people in that town didn’t know what was happening to them. They didn’t know why they were being bombed like this, because they were just in a little civil war that was not that big at the time. I think that we in the world of jazz here in America, we are under attack by those commercial interests…

destructive, that unless somebody understands this and begins to pay attention, jazz is going to disappear from the earth forever, because they have no respect for it. They use it. It’s the foundation of all American popular music. There would be no rock music if there was no jazz music. So they’re base and gross enough to utilize it, but they have no real feeling for it. This concerns me greatly. The record companies have violated the laws of the corporate structure, which is to – first, to serve the society in…
